summary:
Team1 developed A.T.L.A.S. (Black Desert Atlas), an interactive data-driven decision support dashboard evaluating Egypt’s basaltic Black Desert as a terrestrial analog for future lunar south-pole bases and Mars landing sites.

To address the challenge, we integrated open planetary datasets from NASA missions—including MODIS Terra for diurnal Land Surface Temperature, NASA SRTM (30m) for topographic slope profiling across a 9.67 km transect, LRO LOLA & Diviner for lunar polar craters (Shackleton, Haworth, Faustini, Malapert), and MGS MOLA & MEDA for Mars’ Jezero Crater. Moving beyond superficial visual matching, our tool provides interactive thermal filtering, slope distribution metrics (identifying safe touchdown zones under 5°), and transparent cross-planetary benchmarks.

This project is vital because it turns an under-characterized volcanic region into a scientifically documented "natural Earth laboratory," helping mission planners safely test rovers and hardware before costly deep-space deployment.
details:
Project Name: A.T.L.A.S. — Black Desert Atlas (Planetary Analog Discovery)

Project Details:

° What it does & How it works:
Black Desert Atlas is an interactive web-based analytical dashboard designed to evaluate the environmental and topographic suitability of Egypt’s basaltic Black Desert as a terrestrial analog for the Moon and Mars. It operates through four integrated analytical modules:

1. urface Temperature Analytics: Uses NASA MODIS Terra Land Surface Temperature (LST) data (Nov 2025 – Nov 2026) to track diurnal day/night temperature swings, monthly averages, and cloud-masked quality calendars with seasonal filters.

2. errain & Slope Profiling: Analyzes a 9.67 km transect (100 stations at 98m intervals) using NASA SRTM 30m DEM data to compute elevation relief, mean slope, and the percentage of terrain windows under 5° (critical for safe lander touchdown).

3. ross-Planetary Comparison: Benchmarks the Black Desert’s thermal and slope distributions against Jezero Crater on Mars (MGS MOLA & MEDA) and four lunar south-pole targets—Shackleton, Haworth, Faustini, and Malapert—across 2 km and 10 km radial zones (LRO LOLA & Diviner).

4. ata & Methodology Transparency: Documents exact data sources, calculation workflows, and resolution constraints.

° Benefits & Intended Impact:
Provides space agencies and researchers with a scientifically characterized, accessible testbed in Egypt’s Western Desert to validate rovers, landers, and thermal hardware before deep-space missions, significantly reducing testing risks and mission costs.

° Tools, Languages & Technologies Used:

° Data Processing & Geospatial Analysis: Python (Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, GeoPandas, Rasterio)

° Interactive Dashboard & Visualization: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (interactive KPI cards, daily temperature charts, quality heatmaps, elevation/slope transect profiles, and dynamic planetary toggles)

° Data Formats: Standardized CSV datasets derived from official NASA repositories.

° Creative Aspect:
Instead of claiming an unrealistic 100% match between Earth and space, our dashboard emphasizes scientific honesty and interactive exploration. Users can dynamically toggle quality flags, seasonal windows, slope thresholds (<5° and <10°), and lunar radial zones while viewing clear disclaimers regarding resolution differences (30m Earth DEM vs. 463m Mars DEM) and physical boundaries (gravity, atmosphere, radiation).

° Factors Considered by the Team:

1. ata Quality & Cloud Masking: Explicitly separating high-quality MODIS LST observations from cloud gaps and lower-confidence ("other") flags.

2. esolution & Measurement Context: Accounting for spatial resolution differences between Earth (30m) and Mars (463m) datasets, as well as distinguishing mean temperatures from pre-dawn extremes.

3. erification Flags: Clearly flagging specific benchmark values (such as Shackleton 2 km radius metrics) that require further verification before operational mission planning.
